text: The pipeline is built, scheduled, and validated. Now it needs to actually reach someone's screen. This lesson connects Power BI to the Gold table this whole pipeline produces.

Power BI doesn't read Delta files directly off storage — it connects through whichever SQL endpoint the platform exposes. On Azure Databricks, that's Power BI Desktop's Get Data, Azure Databricks connector. On Microsoft Fabric, it's the Lakehouse's own SQL analytics endpoint, reached the same way you'd connect to any SQL database. Different menu, same destination: one small table, one row per day.

Power BI gives you two main ways to connect: Import, which loads a copy of the data and refreshes it on a schedule, or DirectQuery, which sends a live query to the source every time someone opens the report. For a table this size — one row per day, maybe a few hundred rows after a year — Import is the right call. Refreshing something this small costs nothing meaningful, and the report stays fast. DirectQuery earns its complexity on big, high-cardinality fact tables, not a daily summary like this one.

If you're on the Fabric side specifically, there's a third option worth knowing about: Direct Lake, which reads the Delta table's underlying Parquet files straight into Power BI's engine, skipping both Import's refresh cycle and DirectQuery's live round trip. It's not required for this lesson — Import works fine here — but it's worth recognizing by name.

One ordering detail matters regardless of platform: schedule the Power BI refresh to run after last lesson's pipeline job is expected to finish, or the report will silently show yesterday's stale number with no warning. Next lesson, you'll take this connected report and actually present it back to the Store Operations lead.
